Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues? Submitted by Azhar Al-Rubaie on Mon, 09/21/2026 - 08:50 A system created after the 2003 invasion was designed to protect Iraq's oil wealth. More than two decades later, it gives Washington significant leverage over Baghdad A man counts US dollar banknotes at al-Kifah stock market in Baghdad on 27 December 2022 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP) Off For more than two decades, Iraq 's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York. The arrangement, created after the US -led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction. Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran 's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran. The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups. Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "The US decision to freeze or delay sending Iraq's foreign currency entitlements represents a serious violation of the financial and political sovereignty of the Iraqi state," al-Kadhimi said. The shipment was later restored, but the episode demonstrated how Iraq's dependence on the US financial system can be used as a political tool. The arrangement began after the US-led invasion in May 2003, when the Coalition Provisional Authority established the Development Fund for Iraq (DFI) to collect the country's oil revenues and use them for reconstruction and humanitarian needs. Under UN Security Council Resolution 1483, issued in May 2003, Iraqi oil and gas revenues were transferred to a special account in the name of the Central Bank of Iraq at the US Federal Reserve. With US troops departing, Iraq looks beyond balancing Washington and Tehran Read More » Five percent of the revenues were deducted for compensation to Kuwait following Iraq's 1990 invasion. The system also included frozen assets belonging to Saddam Hussein's former government and surplus funds from the UN's Oil-for-Food programme. The arrangement was intended in part to protect Iraqi assets from international creditors pursuing claims dating back to Saddam's rule. An International Advisory and Monitoring Board, including representatives from the UN, IMF, World Bank and Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development, was established to oversee the fund. The UN-backed system ended in 2011 at the request of the Iraqi government but Iraq's oil revenues remained tied to the Federal Reserve. A new account, known as IRAQ2, was established at the New York Fed. Oil revenues are deposited there before being transferred to the Central Bank of Iraq. At the same time, Iraq lost the comprehensive international protection previously provided under the UN system and became dependent on annual US executive orders granting immunity to its sovereign funds. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); So while the formal international arrangement changed, the underlying dependence on the US financial system remained. Why can't Iraq simply move its money? Iraqi oil is priced overwhelmingly in US dollars, while the country depends heavily on the currency for imports and international trade. Iraq also has about $40bn in unsettled external debts, creating concerns that moving its funds outside the existing system could expose them to claims from creditors. Ahmed Saddam, an associate professor of economics at the University of Basra, told Middle East Eye that keeping the Central Bank of Iraq's account in New York has important benefits. "I believe that the most important advantages of keeping the Central Bank of Iraq's account in New York are protecting Iraqi oil revenues from being seized by creditors of the former regime, since the debts are estimated at tens of billions of dollars. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "The second advantage is facilitating the sale of oil and the settlement of Iraq's international trade; this account reduces transfer costs, and we should not forget that the dollar is the most widely used currency in international transactions." But Saddam said the arrangement also leaves Iraq vulnerable to US pressure. 'Financial independence can be achieved by opening multiple sovereign accounts outside the United States while keeping the current account in New York' - Ahmed Saddam, University of Basra "As for the most prominent disadvantages, they lie in the ability of the US authorities to impose their influence by restricting access to dollars to Iraq, for example, and this means there is no real financial independence." According to Saddam, Iraq could sell its oil in euros or Chinese yuan, provided there were no binding conditions in its oil contracts, but even then that would not necessarily free Iraq from the dollar. "Even if that happens, the price will remain linked to the dollar because oil is priced in dollars, and what happens in practice is that the buyer pays the value in a non-dollar currency after converting it according to the dollar exchange rate." Iraq would still need dollars for much of its international trade, Saddam said, while shifting currencies could expose the country to exchange-rate losses and political pressure from Washington. His proposal was therefore diversification rather than an immediate break with the US system. "I believe that Iraq's financial independence will not be achieved if we assume moving the Central Bank of Iraq's account from the United States to another country. "In my view, financial independence can be achieved by opening multiple sovereign accounts outside the United States while keeping the current account in New York. For example, the Central Bank could open an account with the European Central Bank, as well as with central banks in East Asia," Saddam said. "Part of Iraq's oil could also be sold in euros and yuan, let us assume only 15–20 percent, while the remaining 80–85 percent is sold in US dollars. In addition, financial independence requires developing the banking system in Iraq by expanding direct correspondent banking relationships with major banks in Europe and Asia," he added. How is the system being used against Iran? The financial arrangement has taken on greater importance as Washington seeks to squeeze Iran economically and target armed groups in Iraq that are aligned with Tehran. Iraq has close political, economic and security ties with Iran, while several powerful armed groups operate inside the country. For Washington, that has made Iraq's financial system a key battleground in its efforts to restrict the flow of dollars to Iran. The US has accused Iraqi banks, exchange companies and other financial networks of exploiting the country's financial system to move dollars towards sanctioned entities. A quarter-century after the 'war on terror' began, the American Middle East is over Read More » Since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, Washington has responded by tightening its oversight of Iraq's access to the dollar and pressuring Baghdad to bring its financial system into line with US sanctions. In early 2025, Iraq ended its long-running dollar auction system, formally known as the foreign currency window, after sustained US pressure. The system had allowed private banks and exchange companies to obtain dollars from the Central Bank of Iraq in exchange for Iraqi dinars. But Washington's leverage extends beyond Iraq's banking system to the physical movement of dollars into the country. The April suspension of the $500m shipment was particularly significant because the cash was generated from Iraq's own oil revenues. Although electronic dollar transfers for international trade continued, the episode showed that Washington could restrict access to physical dollars when it wanted to pressure Baghdad. The Iraqi government has sought to maintain its relationship with Washington while balancing its ties with Tehran and Iran-aligned armed groups. Iraq's Oil Minister Basem Mohammed Khudhair refused to answer questions about moving away from the Federal Reserve, telling MEE that the question fell under the remit of the finance ministry. However, he described the relationship between Baghdad and Washington as positive. "There has been dialogue with the United States - a very positive dialogue, especially after our trip accompanied by the Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi there," he said. "There is great understanding between the Iraqi government and the American government, and the US has provided all support to the Iraqi government for its success in its economic and political dossiers." But the consequences of Iraq's financial dependence are ultimately felt beyond government ministries and central banks. 'US controls Iraq's fate' Hussein Ali, a 35-year-old Baghdad native, said removing US oversight would not necessarily improve the lives of ordinary Iraqis. "For us, whether Iraq's money goes to the Federal Reserve in America or comes directly to Iraq, I don't think our situation as citizens will improve. "Instead, the money will be at the disposal of the corrupt, and financial corruption will be even greater than it is now. From my viewpoint, I find it better for the money to remain in New York, under the guardianship and oversight of the US banking authorities." Ali nevertheless acknowledged the sovereignty problem. 'Whether Iraq's money goes to the Federal Reserve in America or comes directly to Iraq, I don't think our situation as citizens will improve' - Hussein Ali, Baghdad native "It is true that keeping Iraq's money in the US bank gives the United States the freedom to control Iraq's fate politically, financially and in sovereign terms. He also raised concerns about money being moved towards Iran. "We have often heard how many officials and not state people smuggle money to Iran to help it confront the American economic blockade on Iran. Imagine what would happen if Iraq received its oil sale money into Iraqi banks far from American oversight and auditing. I believe Iraq's situation will only get worse." Fatima Abdulkarim, a 55-year-old from Basra, shared those concerns. "I do not believe that Iraq's oil funds going to Iraq directly instead of going to US banks will help to improve our economic situation. "Yes, it means Iraqis would dispose of the money without direct US intervention, but corruption will be greater, and the money will go to the same corrupt parties and officials. If the money remains in New York, it is at least under oversight and auditing. But if it comes to Iraqi banks far from any real oversight, I believe Iraq's situation will be worse off." "Keeping the money under the guardianship and oversight of the US banking authorities is better than it reaching the hands of the corrupt," Abdulkarim said. Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues? For more than two decades, Iraq 's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York. The arrangement, created after the US -led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction. Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran 's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran. The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups. Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds. The authorities later announced legal proceedings against the organisers over violations of Iran’s mandatory dress rules. But for the runners themselves, at least for those interviewed for this story by Middle East Eye, that morning was about something more ordinary: just running. Fahimeh, a psychologist who took part in the race, described the atmosphere as a rare experience of energy, hope and life. That choice is difficult to understand without looking at what has happened to Iran's sense of the future in recent years. The impact of two wars in consecutive years, and the possibility of another round of military conflict, have become deeply visible in everyday life. Decades of sanctions and economic restrictions have eroded purchasing power, while inflation, unemployment and rising housing costs have made many long-term plans increasingly difficult. Political disappointments and restrictions on everyday life have added another layer of uncertainty. Many people simply no longer ask whether the future will be better. Instead, they wonder whether it can still be planned for at all. But that would be too simple a reading. People at both gatherings had arrived with friends, family members, acquaintances or colleagues. There was a sense of dynamism and excitement at each, and those taking part likely shared many of the same concerns about their families, jobs, finances and the future. Yet for many Iranians, the scale of those expectations has changed. Hamed, a journalist and father of a teenager, describes hope as “the last asset a person has”. He said difficult economic conditions have not necessarily extinguished people’s hopes, but have changed what they hope for. A home or a car may once have represented a realistic aspiration. Now, that same desire may take a more modest form: buying a new phone, taking a short trip, going to a cafe or finding an inexpensive way to spend time with family. For Hamed, these choices still matter because they show that people are making plans, even when those plans have become smaller. Elsewhere in Tehran, Maryam, a sports and dance instructor, sees a similar instinct in the people who continue to attend her classes. But the economic crisis has also hit the industry hard. Fewer people can afford classes, and there is a limit to what families can spend on activities that are not essential to survival. Yet some continue. Maryam says there are many reasons why. Dance brings pleasure through music and rhythm, provides physical activity, and allows people to develop a skill. It can also bring people together and offer a break from the pressures of everyday life. Maryam considers learning a skill a form of investment. People spend money learning languages, music or other skills because they expect them to remain useful throughout their lives. Dance, she says, is no different. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); That belief is also what drives her to keep teaching. Her students have kept practising through periods of political unrest and war, including times when classes had to move online. For them, that is what it means to remain hopeful for better days to come. Building a life anyway In Tehran’s Grand Bazaar, Reza, a car dealer and trader, reflects on the path his life has taken. He believes the person he has chosen is right for him, and describes their union as an investment in the future – a chance to build a home together, experience something different and work towards the life they want. The uncertainty, he said, is unavoidable. He does not believe the future is secure. The Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints north of Ramallah, along with the Jaba’ checkpoint northeast of Jerusalem, stand out as prominent examples of checkpoints characterised by long waiting times, particularly during peak hours. These checkpoints slow the movement of Palestinians between villages, towns and cities, with delays often extending further depending on inspection procedures and conditions at the site, thereby creating major bottlenecks on routes used daily by thousands of Palestinians. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Attaf Abu Aliya, a taxi driver from the village of al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah, said he is forced to wait hours every day at checkpoints that soldiers frequently set up at the village entrance. Under normal circumstances, the trip from al-Mughayyir to Ramallah takes only 30 minutes, but the tightened closure has turned the journey into an ordeal lasting many hours. "Waiting for hours has become the norm; soldiers stand there without conducting searches or allowing vehicles to pass, simply to make our lives miserable,” Abu Aliya told Middle East Eye. “Students miss university classes, and everyone's affairs are disrupted, all because of the whim of a single soldier," he added. Abu Aliya said the situation becomes even more difficult when settlers take control of the checkpoint. 'Waiting for hours has become the norm' - Attaf Abu Aliya, Palestinian taxi driver At times, he said, settlers stop vehicles, block passage, smash windows and spray pepper spray at passengers waiting to cross. Abu Aliya said he has been searched and beaten by soldiers several times while waiting at the checkpoint. Waiting for more than four hours a day has become routine, he said. “Our situation is truly tragic. That is the most accurate description of the lockdown and the tightened restrictions we are facing,” he explained. Ambulance delays According to data published on 25 September by the Commission Against the Wall and Settlements, the West Bank now has 942 checkpoints, closure points and other obstacles. The figure includes 824 permanent checkpoints and closure points, as well as 118 barriers such as earth mounds, trenches and roadblocks. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The United Nations says the restrictions extend beyond existing checkpoints. New obstacles have been erected in recent months, further disrupting movement between Palestinian communities. The restrictions are also hampering ambulance crews and medical teams, who need rapid access to patients across the West Bank. Israel attacking hospitals and blocking medical aid in the West Bank, warns MSF Read More » With village and town entrances closed, and checkpoints causing lengthy delays, paramedics are facing growing difficulties reaching emergencies and transporting patients to hospital. Ahmed Jibril, director of the Emergency Medical Services Department at the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, said ambulances are given no priority or special status, and are often subjected to stricter checks. Last week, an ambulance crew was unable to reach an elderly woman near Salfit because of closed checkpoints and iron gates, Jibril said. US, Iran may return to table within days over Hormuz. • Trump claims negotiators to engage Iranians this week, says he turned down an earlier proposal • Araghchi says Iran ready to open strait if ceasefire deal revived, frozen assets released • Pentagon denies IRGC claims of capturing US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz; Guards warn Washington against staging fresh attacks WASHINGTON/TEHRAN: The Uni­ted States and Iran are expected to hold talks this week, said President Donald Trump after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East and a return to the conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart a few months ago. President Trump told Axios that his negotiators would engage their Iranian counterpart over the next few days apparently to break the stalemate over Hormuz. Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. It called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, and a return to the conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart a few months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran has never closed the door to diplomacy but it would not capitulate. “Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” Mr Araghchi posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.” ‘Demanding too much’ President Trump, however, said Iranians were losing badly, which was the reason they wanted to make a deal to open the strait. “They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine. I like making a deal too.” His ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table. “This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk,” he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday. The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials. It said Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections. Despite Trump’s public statements, mediators facilitating Tehran’s talks with Washington have not officially relayed a US rejection of the plan, the Iranian top diplomat said. “We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” Mr Araghchi noted. ‘Critical, decisive stage’ At the same time, Iran’s armed forces said they were prepared for any renewed US attacks. Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia warned that the US would suffer greater damage if it launched another attack on his country. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed on Sunday to have seized an American submarine drone on Sunday in the strategic Strait of Hormuz. They said that the drone was “operating in the Strait of Hormuz for espionage purposes”, identifying the model as a Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle that was “now in the hands of the force’s specialists for data recovery”. Separately, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami said the war was at a critical and decisive stage, adding that Tehran would not accept a situation in which it was unable to trade while foreign powers used the region’s strategic waterways. “If Iran cannot trade, if Iran cannot live, no one will be able to trade or live,” he added. Country braces for 25pc Rabi water shortage. • Reservoir carryover falls below 9.5MAF, lowest since 2021 • Wheat crop faces added pressure after estimated shortfall last season • Irsa technical committee to finalise Rabi water availability, provincial shares • Three-tier water distribution formula may revive acrimony among traditional rivals Sindh, Punjab ISLAMABAD: After many years, Pakistan is bracing for a water shortage of around 25 per cent during the Rabi season starting this week, raising concerns about food security next year as wheat is the season’s main crop. The last Rabi season faced no water shortage, yet the country is estimated to have suffered a wheat shortfall of more than two million tonnes. This forced the government to order imports of one million tonnes, including 750,000 tonnes in the first phase for delivery in November. Against a production target of 29.7m tonnes and consumption req­uirements of 31.9m tonnes, the country is estimated to have produced around 27.5m tonnes as far­mers faced challenging conditions following changes in wheat policy. Part of the estimated Rabi water shortage is man-made, owing to the political needs of the coalition government, informed sources told Dawn , adding that more than one million acre feet (MAF) of avoidable water releases were made from reservoirs during the outgoing Kharif season. The sources said parliamentary interventions had allowed higher discharges to Sindh with commitments for subsequent adjustments in provincial shares, which could not be materialised within the Kharif season. Total storage in the two major reservoirs peaked at 11.6MAF on Sept 9, when Tarbela remained full at its 5.8MAF capacity bet­ween Aug 9 and Sept 9 while Mangla touched 5.733MAF on Sept 9. Both reservoirs started depleting since then, with total storage falling below 9.5MAF ahead of the Rabi season — the lowest carryover since 2021. Rabi begins on Oct 1 and generally ends on March 31. Last year, the season started with a healthy carryover of 13MAF in the reservoirs, almost 27pc higher than this year. Wheat is the largest Rabi crop, while gram, lentil, tobacco, rapeseed, barley and mustard are among the other crops grown during the season. The sources said Rabi 2024 had started with carryover storage of 10.5MAF and the country faced a water shortage of 15-18pc, while Rabi 2023 began with 11.6MAF. Rabi 2022 started with 9.5MAF, when the country faced a 20-22pc shortage. Rabi 2021 was the worst among recent years, beginning with 7.42MAF in reservoir storage and resulting in a 28pc shortage. Against this backdrop, the technical committee of the Indus River System Authority (Irsa) will meet on Monday (today) to finalise water availability estimates and recommend criteria for distribution among the provinces for the Rabi cropping season. The Irsa Advisory Committee (IAC) has also been tentatively called to meet on Oct 5 to approve provincial water shares on the recommendations of the technical committee. The anticipated shortages are likely to revive provincial acrimony, particularly between Sindh and Punjab, as Irsa seeks to allocate water under the three-tier formula it uses to manage shortages. Tarbela Dam reached its maximum conservation level of 1,550 feet on Aug 9 and remained there until Sept 9. Mangla Dam peaked at 1,222 feet on Aug 9 against its maximum conservation level of 1,242 feet. Flows in the Jhelum River remained weak throughout the Kharif season, while subsequent rel­e­a­ses further reduced Man­gla’s conservation level. As a result, Mangla’s storage stood at 5.12MAF on Sunday night against its maximum storage capacity of 7.277MAF. Mangla had reached 1,233.25 feet at the end of Kharif 2023 and 1,224 feet in 2025. Around 10.33MAF of water has flowed into the sea since the Kharif season began on April 1 against an annual environmental requirement of about 8.2MAF. Total water requirements for Rabi crops under the Water Apportionment Accord of 1991 are about 37-38MAF. With limited carryover storage from Kharif, water availability is expected to be around 21-22MAF, along with river flows over the next six months. The accord empowers Irsa to determine the country’s water availability and provincial shares twice a year. The 1991 water accord works well in rare cases of sufficient annual water availability of 114MAF. However, with shortages exceeding 10pc becoming increasingly common, Irsa has been using a de facto three-tier formula for distributing provincial shares — a mechanism opposed by Sindh, which has been pushing for implementation of Para 2 of the accord. Irsa has maintained for several years that it cannot change the existing distribution mechanism used to absorb shortages. Under Para 2 of the 1991 accord, provincial water shares were fixed. However, amid persistent shortages, Irsa, with the involvement of the federal and provincial governments, introduced a cascading distribution mechanism in 2002. The three-tier formula now combines Para 2, Para 14(a) and historical water use from 1977 to 1982. Para 14(b) requires that 10 daily uses be adjusted pro rata to correspond with seasonal allocations of different canal systems and form the basis for sharing shortages and surpluses across the country. Under the three-tier formula, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa are exempt from shortages, leaving the shortfall to be shared by Sindh and Punjab. However, Sindh maintains that it bears a disproportionately larger shortage under this mechanism. The province has argued that Irsa exceeded its mandate by introducing the three-tier formula and devised its own formulas despite Sindh’s objection through a meeting of the provincial committee of ministers. When asked about the incident, Mr Channar alleged that some people had disrupted polling and were found stamping ballot papers in favour of his rival. He claimed that the individuals were expelled following the scuffle and that polling resumed after remaining suspended for several hours. Meanwhile, some voters at the Bahawalpur 3-Marla Housing Scheme polling station alleged police officials deployed there had not allowed voters whose CNICs carried addresses from the Yazman area, which is considered a stronghold of Mr Cheema, to cast their ballots. PM congratulates party candidate Later, a statement issued by PM Office said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif congratulated Malik Munir Iqbal Channar as well as his brother Malik Zaheer Iqbal Channar, who is incumbent Punjab Assembly deputy speaker, on the victory in the by-election. The PM lauded the people of Bahawalpur for electing their representative, stating that the victory showed public confidence in the PML-N. Imran Gabol in Lahore also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, September 28th, 2026

PTI dares govt to impose governor’s rule in KP. • Panjutha warns move would further deteriorate situation in province; Shahid Khattak proposes assembly resignations, street protests • KP speaker asks police chief to provide details of arrested, detained MPAs ISLAMABAD/PESHAWAR: Amid rising demand in the Centre for the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, senior PTI leader Naeem Haider Panjutha has challenged the federal government to go ahead with the move, warning that it would further deteriorate the situation in the province. “You have already stolen the people’s mandate, stripped them of their two-thirds majority and reserved seats, filed thousands of politically motivated cases, imprisoned tens of thousands, including Imran Khan, raided homes, violated the sanctity of chadar and chardiwari, and imprisoned women, including Bushra Bibi and Imran Khan’s sisters,” Advocate Naeem Haider Panjutha said while talking to Dawn. Mr Swati informed the police chief that, being the custodian of the House, he had directed the assembly secretariat to obtain information about any member of the KP Assembly, minister, adviser, special assistant to the chief minister or parliamentary secretary who had been arrested or detained. Pakistan advance to Asian Games cricket semi-finals after rain washes out Hong Kong clash. Persistent rain forced the abandonment of Pakistan’s cricket quarter-final against Hong Kong without a ball being bowled on Monday, allowing the national side to progress to the semi-finals of the Asian Games on the basis of their superior ICC Twenty20 International ranking. The first quarter-final, scheduled at Korogi Sports Park, was called off at the time of the toss after incessant showers left large parts of the ground under covers. Officials determined there was no realistic chance of play, even in a heavily reduced format. Pakistan, one of four seeded teams alongside India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh that received a direct entry into the last eight, advanced under tournament regulations that award the higher-ranked side progression in the event of a no-result. Hong Kong, ranked significantly lower, exited the competition without taking the field. Hong Kong had reached the quarter-finals by finishing second in Group ‘B’ having defeated Malaysia by eight wickets before suffering a 41-run loss to Oman. Pakistan had arrived in Japan after a training camp in Karachi and a practice session in Nisshin that was also disrupted by overnight rain and a wet outfield. The side, captained by Sahibzada Farhan and coached by Mike Hesson, will face the winners of Tuesday’s quarter-final between Bangladesh and Malaysia in the semi-finals, scheduled for Thursday at the same venue. This would have been the third T20 meeting between the two sides, with Pakistan having prevailed in both previous encounters at the 2022 Asia Cup and the 2023 Asian Games. Pakistan won bronze in the men’s cricket event at the 2010 Asian Games. The second quarter-final between India and Afghanistan, scheduled to be the later fixture at the same venue was also abandoned without a ball bowled due to rain. India, being the higher-ranked side, advanced to the semi-finals where they will meet the winners of the quarter-final between Sri Lanka and Nepal. The semi-finals are set for October 1, with the bronze-medal match and final scheduled for October 3.

China to cut tariffs on US farm goods, but list excludes soya beans. China is set to cut tariffs on a broad range of US agricultural goods, from corn and wheat to meat and dairy, but top import item soybeans were excluded from a tariff-reduction list jointly issued by China’s commerce ministry and the White House. Markets have been waiting for news on Chinese tariff cuts on US farm goods following last week’s Washington summit of leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. The agricultural tariff cuts are part of the $60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts negotiated by the Board of Trade and unveiled for the first time on Monday. The list covers sorghum, vegetable oils and meals, including soya oil and soya meal, along with meat, dairy products and other items. While the proposal identifies the covered products, it does not specify when the tariff cuts will take effect. More than 90 per cent of the covered products will be exempt from all additional tariffs imposed on each other and will instead be subject to most-favoured-nation tariff rates, the commerce ministry said in a statement. US soybeans, however, still face an additional tariff of 10pc, which traders have warned is too high for private crushers to absorb, even as Chinese state buyers have stepped up purchases. “Despite the soybean being a non-sensitive item in trade, the political significance of China’s soybean purchase is enormous and carries major political implications,” said Feng Chucheng, founder and partner at Hutong Research. Keeping soya beans on a separate track gives Beijing leverage in its dealings with Washington, especially ahead of the US midterm elections, Feng added. Chinese state-run agricultural companies Sinograin and COFCO have bought more than 12 million metric tons of US soya beans, nearly half the 25 million the White House has said Beijing committed to buying annually through 2028. Trade in the agricultural and related products on Monday’s list stood at about $17 billion in 2024, roughly matching China’s reported purchase commitment, excluding soya beans, according to Reuters calculations. In May, the White House said Beijing had agreed to buy that volume annually through 2028, but China has yet to confirm any target for such purchases. State-run companies will continue to buy US soya beans and the tariff cuts on other goods will help China meet the $17 billion commitment, said a trader based in Asia with an international company that sells soya beans to China who spoke on condition of anonymity. Without tariffs, the landed cost for both US and Brazilian beans is roughly $595 per ton, although Brazilian soya beans are generally preferred for their higher oil and protein content, according to traders. At those prices, Chinese private crushers are running at negative margins. The most-active soya bean contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) was trading down 1.38pc at $13-3/4 per bushel as of 0709 GMT.

3 traffic policemen martyred in attack on vehicle in KP's Tank. DERA ISMAIL KHAN: Three traffic policemen were martyred when unidentified armed men opened fire on their mobile van in the Wazirabad Bazaar area of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Tank district, a senior police official confirmed. “Three traffic policemen travelling in the mobile van were martyred on the spot in the attack,” District Police Officer Abdul Samad Khan told Dawn , adding that the attackers fled the scene. Khan said the attackers had also taken away the traffic police vehicle after the incident. However, the vehicle was later recovered from the Garah Budha area, he added. He added that two passers-by were also injured in the firing and were shifted to a hospital for treatment. “Police have sealed the roads and other possible routes, including pedestrian tracks, to prevent the attackers from escaping,” the DPO told Dawn . Mir Raza murder case: Judicial commission proceedings adjourned as 30-day tenure ends. KARACHI: Proceedings of the judicial commission investigating the Mir Raza Ali murder case could not proceed on Monday after its 30-day tenure expired, with a request for an extension until Oct 15 awaiting a decision by the Sindh cabinet. According to the order sheet available with Dawn , the commission was informed that Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah had approved the summary seeking the extension and forwarded it to the provincial cabinet for a decision. The cabinet is expected to meet on Oct 1, the order sheet said, adding that “it was therefore appropriate to adjourn Monday’s proceedings until Oct 2 at 10am”. The order sheet said that if the cabinet decided not to extend the commission’s tenure, no further witnesses would be called and the report would shortly thereafter be submitted on the basis of the statements recorded so far. However, if the cabinet approved the extension, fresh notices would be issued to the witnesses. A questionnaire for three senior police officers would also be sent on Oct 2, it added. On Saturday, the commission had dismissed an application filed by the deceased’s family seeking the personal appearance of the Karachi police chief and the head of the investigation team before the commission. Last week, the judicial commission declined a request by Dr Osama Shaikh, the medico-legal officer who conducted Ali’s first autopsy, to record a further statement. In its order, the commission said it had enough information to determine the facts and circumstances of the case and attribute any negligence. It also cautioned investor Ahmed Bhardey against attempting to derail the proceedings through media statements. The commission had earlier questioned discrepancies in Dr Shaikh’s post-mortem reports. Ali’s body was later exhumed and a second autopsy was conducted, which concluded that he had been shot in the back and ruled out suicide. The case so far Ali’s body was found a day after he went missing on July 28. Since then, the case has been mired in controversy, with the deceased’s family accusing the police of trying to bury the facts while the investigators initially attempted to build the case around the possibility of a suicide. Days after the recovery of Ali’s body on July 29, Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir, accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death, while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered under charges of kidnapping. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, the counsel for Ali’s family approached the SHC, objecting to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and seeking the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case”. On Sept 2, the SHC dismissed that petition filed by Ali’s family, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”. Meanwhile, the final report of Ali’s second post-mortem for the Mir Raza Ali murder case confirmed that his death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back. “Death occurred due to cardiac rupture consequent to perforating firearm injury of the chest,” the report stated, adding that the entry wound was on the posterior thorax (back) and the exit wound on the anterior thorax (front of the chest). “The findings are inconsistent with suicide as the manner of death,” it confirmed.

Minister slams KP govt’s ‘flaws’ in leadership, resources and authority in counter-terror fight. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry on Monday said the PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had not made adequate efforts to combat terrorism, particularly highlighting flaws in its leadership, resources and use of authority. Addressing media in Islamabad alongside Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Chaudhry noted that a political leadership could “provide three things in the fight against terrorism: leadership, resources and powers”. He contended that the provincial administration in KP — where the PTI has been in power since 2013 — “did not provide leadership to the security forces over the past 14 years”. The interior official accused the PTI-led government of “creating space” for terrorists. “If Pakistan is burning in the fire of terrorism, it is because of KP’s incompetent leadership,” he maintained. Chaudhry then noted that it was the provincial government’s responsibility to allocate funds for counter-terrorism in the budget. “[Then], why did you not provide the resources?” he asked, adding that the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) was still not functional in the entire province. “Your forces cannot fight unarmed. You do not have bulletproof jackets, cars, training, CTD, Safe City [project], or a forensic lab,” he said, claiming that Safe City projects had been completed on the tehsil level as well in Punjab. The state minister sought accountability from KP over the usage of even one per cent of the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award, which he said amounted to Rs800 billion. Chaudhry pointed out that KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and his information minister did not attend the funeral prayers of the victims of the Sept 18 Kohat blast , but were rather “busy in their street movement or other matters”. He recalled that the KP CM held a “very lengthy” press conference in Dera Ismail Khan in the wake of Saturday’s suicide blast , which claimed 12 lives. “Why did they not condemn Afghanistan? Why do you have a soft attitude on Afghanistan? Why do you deliberately employ such ambiguity and demeanour, and do not openly condemn or name the real enemy or from where these proxies operate?” he asked. Chaudhry reiterated his criticism of the recent KP Police Act , which has been proposed to replace a 2017 version and is aimed at curtailing the powers of the provincial inspector general (IG). He also responded to PTI’s allegation that the party had not been included in discussions about war on terrorism, saying that the party leadership did not show up to meetings when invited. “You come to Islamabad to demand NFC funds , but your CM does not show up for anti-terrorism meetings,” Chaudhry said. Meanwhile, Tarar said PTI had not taken ownership of the fight against terrorism, again terming the party as the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan’s (TTP) “B team”. He alleged that PTI had facilitated terrorists in its over 12 years of governing KP and that it was not condemning them as it “suits PTI’s financial interests”. “Sohail Afridi organised a ceremony and two Afghans did not stand up to pay respect to the national anthem. If I was there, I would have dealt with them right then and there. I would have banned them,” Tarar said. Such an incident took place in September 2024 , when PTI’s Ali Amin Gandapur was serving as the chief minister. Tarar went on to highlight that the KP government had not ensured the registration of all vehicles yet, as doing so makes the “surveillance of terrorists easier”. He added that potential revenue generated from car registration could have been used for the benefit of the people of KP. “You sacrificed the security of the entire province for your political gains. “You will now have to decide if you are with Pakistan or with Afghanistan. It is as clear as that,” the information minister declared. Afghanistan’s ‘true face’ At the outset of the press conference, Chaudhry noted that terrorist “proxies are financed by our eastern border and their hideouts are on the western border”. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. He emphasised that Islamabad had employed “every way” to convey its concerns to Kabul, including dialogue, dossiers and international forums, but to no avail. Referring to the recent attack on a rescue vehicle carrying DI Khan blast victims, Chaudhry said that attacking rescue teams was not allowed even during war. “This is their true face. Is this jihad? Even an enemy with some rules does not carry out such attacks.” He said such terrorist activities were carried out in exchange for receiving funds in dollars, which were proportional to the number of casualties. The interior official asserted that Pakistan had the “best systems” for investigating the identity of a suspected terrorist. “Very few countries have enough data that in less than a minute, any heinous crime or terrorist incident-related information can be accessed in Nadra and other databases […] we instantly find out whether they are Pakistanis [or not].” He then recalled that when authorities did not find any details in the database for a recent incident, they used open-source intelligence and geolocated a terrorist’s picture to Kabul’s Pashtunistan Square. September witnessed another bout of conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with the former saying it struck terrorist sites in the border region in response to a recent spate of terrorist attacks . Pakistan conducted “aerial and drone strikes” in another 10 locations across Afghanistan in retaliation for drones launched from across the border that were shot down in KP. The Foreign Office (FO) has said a demarche was also delivered to the Afghan side on Saturday on account of the Sept 23 airspace violation by drones.

Pakistan volleyball captain criticises Asian Games logistics after another win; hockey side thrash Oman. Pakistan volleyball captain Murad Jehan criticised the organisers of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday after his team were taken to the wrong venue shortly before their Pool ‘A’ match against Uzbekistan, while Pakistan’s hockey side finished their pool campaign with a commanding 7-2 victory over Oman. The volleyball team were taken to the wrong gymnasium by their bus driver, leaving the players with little time to warm up before the match. In a video posted on Instagram, a visibly frustrated Murad described the episode as “another mismanagement” and said players had been forced to change into their playing kits on the moving bus. “We have a very important match and the bus driver doesn’t know which gymnasium we are going to play,” he said. “He took a wrong way and came to a wrong gymnasium and now we are short of time. Complaints about logistics have been a recurring feature of the Games, with the chief organiser apologising on Saturday for widespread operational glitches. Pakistan completed their Asian Games hockey pool campaign with a commanding 7-2 victory over Oman, recovering from their defeat by Malaysia to finish the group stage strongly and keep their medal hopes alive. Pakistan could not break the deadlock in the first quarter, with Sufyan missing from a penalty corner before Oman goalkeeper Ibrahim Al Farsi saved efforts from Hannan Shahid, Abu Mahmood and Sufyan as the opening period ended goalless. Al Farsi denied Hannan and Rana again early in the second, but penalty corner specialist Sufyan finally broke through in the 22nd minute. Oman shocked Pakistan when Al Baraa Al Nofli equalised in the 27th, only for Sufyan to strike again from a penalty corner barely a minute later. Pakistan added three more in the third quarter. Rana’s shot was saved early, but he got on the scoresheet in the 34th minute from a penalty corner. Oman pressed for a way back, with efforts from Aliyas Al-Noufali, Maitham Al Wahaibi and Rashad Al Fazari kept out before Aiman Madit finally scored in the 36th. Ghazanfar then restored Pakistan’s two-goal cushion with a field goal, and Rana added another from a penalty corner in the 44th. Irish players refuse handshakes, wear black armbands in Nation Leagues clash against Israel. Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in a Nations League clash on Sunday amid an eerie and sombre atmosphere that saw the Irish players wear black armbands over the war in Gaza. Ireland’s players also bowed their heads as the Israeli national anthem was played at the near-empty Debrecen stadium in Hungary. The teams skipped the traditional pre-match handshakes and did not exchange pennants either. Troy Parrott made a heart sign with his hands after opening the scoring on 14 minutes, while Jack Moylan kissed the Irish badge on his jersey and his black armband after netting the third goal 25 minutes in. Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson said his team had “raised awareness worldwide” about the Gaza conflict after they chose not to shake hands with Israeli players. The game, in which Israel were the nominal hosts, had been in doubt earlier in the week until Ireland’s players voted overwhelmingly to fulfil the fixture, despite pressure from back home to boycott the match. Only one player, goalkeeper Gavin Buzunu, pulled out, saying “it would be wrong to participate” in either this match or the return fixture in Serbia on October 4 due to the “killing of innocent people”. “It has been so difficult for so many players,” Icelander Hallgrimsson told broadcaster RTE after the game. “I hope that will not be in the next game because they have shown support to the protest, they have raised awareness worldwide, not only in Ireland, on the subject and that is normally the reason for protesting, to raise awareness of a situation. “I think these players have done that with all their actions, with all that they have been saying. No more than Gavin Bazunu, but the others have done it here on the pitch and how they have shown their actions, so I hope people understand that.” Since Ireland were drawn in the same Nations League group as Israel in February, prominent Irish figures including sportspeople, fan groups and pro-Palestinian campaigners have protested against the matches going ahead. The Irish federation did not reserve any tickets for fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE was due to show it without commentary. Israeli minister irked Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused Ireland of being “on the wrong side of history” over the players’ actions. In a lengthy post on X, Saar referenced the Irish team of 1939 giving the Nazi salute ahead of a match against Germany in Bremen. He also referred to Irish neutrality during the Second World War and the condolences offered by then-prime minister Eaemon de Valera to the German representative in Dublin following Adolf Hitler’s death. “Almost 90 years have passed. Ireland’s unique talent for finding itself on the wrong side of history remains intact,” he added. “Sports, soccer, basketball, everything is for the public, the people, and not for politics,” 31-year-old software development teacher Mol Michael, draped in an Israeli scarf, told AFP . “Once you decide, because of politics, to cancel the Irish audience, this is a really stupid move from Ireland, in my opinion.” Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy often linked to the country’s own history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway, and has repeatedly criticised Israel over its relentless bombardment of Gaza.

Lahore ATC extends physical remand of PTI's Hammad Azhar for 7 days in Jinnah House attack case. LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Monday extended the physical remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar for another seven days in the 2023 Jinnah House attack case . Sarwar Road police had booked several PTI leaders and workers on charges of attacking and vandalising the Jinnah House , which also serves as the residence of the corps commander, during the May 9, 2023 protests against the arrest of ex-premier Imran Khan. On Monday, police produced the former federal finance minister before ATC Judge Manzer Ali Gill upon the completion of his 21-day physical remand . During the hearing, a state prosecutor said police needed further remand to recover the suspect’s mobile phone and SIM, describing them as important pieces of evidence. He urged the court to extend the remand for a further seven days. Speaking before the court, Azhar questioned why further remand was being sought, saying he had already been kept on physical remand for 21 days in an alleged occurrence where he said he was not even present. “Even a murder suspect is sent on 14-day remand here. Has my offence become more serious than murder?” he asked. The former minister also complained that he had earlier not been allowed to meet his lawyers or family members — a concern also voiced earlier by his family before a court. The ATC then reserved its decision on the prosecution’s request for further remand, and later announced its decision, granting the police Azhar’s remand for another seven days. Meeting with family allowed, LHC told Separately, a two-member Lahore High Court (LHC) bench headed by Justice Syed Shahbaz Ali Rizvi disposed of a petition filed by Azhar’s mother and wife against the alleged denial of access to him during police custody. A Lahore ATC had already disposed of a similar plea filed by the family, directing them to approach the police on the matter. A Punjab government lawyer informed the LHC bench that Azhar had been allowed to meet his mother and wife. The law officer further said that the PTI leader would also meet his lawyer at the trial court on Monday. Relying on the government lawyer’s statement, the bench disposed of the petition. According to his family , Azhar was arrested on Sept 5. However, police said the next day they were unaware of his arrest, prompting the PTI leader’s mother to approach the LHC on Sept 7, and he was produced before an ATC the same day. Azhar, the son of late former Punjab governor Mian Muhammad Azhar , has been declared a proclaimed offender by multiple anti-terrorism courts for not joining the proceedings against him in cases related to the May 9 riots . Azhar had reappeared in public on May 22, 2024, a year after he had gone into hiding when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership following the violent incidents of May 9 . At the time, the PTI leader had evaded arrest when the Counter-Terrorism Department raided the party’s secretariat in Islamabad.

Special delivery: India's Tamil Nadu state hands out gold for newborns. Authorities in India’s Tamil Nadu state gave babies born in government-run hospitals a free gold ring on Monday, an initiative aimed at boosting confidence in the public healthcare system. Under the scheme launched by actor-turned-Chief Minister Vijay, all babies born in public health facilities in the state are eligible for a one-gramme gold ring, worth some $143. Gold has immense cultural significance in India, featuring prominently in weddings and religious ceremonies, and seen as a safe generational asset. “The gold ring would give the child something valuable to keep for the years ahead,” said one mother at a government hospital in the state’s Madurai district, who declined to give her name. She was among dozens of mothers who cradled their newborns as they queued up to receive the gift. “This scheme feels personal,” another grateful mother, Stella Mary, told AFP. Officials say the initiative aims to highlight maternal and newborn care, while strengthening faith in public healthcare institutions in the southern state of over 72 million people. The scheme, however, drew some criticism from the Bharatiya Janata Party, which is in the opposition in Tamil Nadu. “A gold ring for a newborn may be a welcome gesture, but for families, the most immediate need is ensuring that essential nutrition is available every day,” party member Tamilisai Soundararajan said in a social media post. India’s overcrowded public hospitals often struggle with staff shortages, long waiting times and patchy infrastructure, prompting many patients to seek treatment in the costly private sector. While most women in India give birth in hospitals, home deliveries still occur in some rural communities, making institutional childbirth a priority for health authorities. Despite significant gains in recent years, infant and maternal mortality rates continue to languish in India. The country recorded 24 infant deaths per 1,000 live births while maternal deaths stood at 88 per 100,000 live births, according to latest official data. The gold ring scheme, known as the “Thaimaman” (maternal uncle) programme, draws on the special cultural significance of a child’s maternal uncle, who is often expected to play a key role in family milestones and celebrations. It also taps into India’s enduring obsession with gold. For many women, particularly in rural areas, gold jewellery can serve as a form of personal financial security. India is one of the world’s largest consumers of the metal. According to the World Gold Council, demand in the country reached $25 billion in the first quarter of this year.

Heavy rain lashes twin cities as civic departments put on alert. RAWALPINDI: Islamabad and Rawalpindi received a fresh spell of rain on Monday, with civic departments in Rawalpindi placed on high alert on the commissioner’s orders. The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) recorded 33mm of rain at Saidpur village on Monday morning. Golra, near E-11, received 25mm of rain, while Pirwadhai and Gawalmandi recorded 28mm and 27mm, respectively. According to PMD data, 23mm of rain was recorded in H-8, 22mm in I-12 and 29mm in Shamsabad. In its update, the PMD advised residents to stay away from Nullah Lai. “Nullah Lai is being continuously monitored, and the public is being kept informed in a timely manner,” Rawalpindi Commissioner Salman Ghani said. The water flow is currently normal, according to the authorities. The water level in Nullah Lai stands at 5.5 feet at Katarian and 2 feet at Gawalmandi. In a post on X, the Islamabad Traffic Police said its officers were ensuring a smooth flow of traffic and urged residents to adhere to traffic advisories and cooperate with the police. Heavy rain caused two flight diversions, Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) said. Furthermore, an AirSial flight from Jeddah to Islamabad was diverted to Peshawar due to “bad weather”, landing at 10:25am, PAA said. Citizens were urged to contact the district administration or the Wasa helpline in case of an emergency. The National Disaster Management Authority has, meanwhile, released a report detailing casualties and damages recorded in rain-related incidents between June 26 and Sept 28. Among the deaths, 80 were reported from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 70 from Punjab, 19 from Sindh, seven from Azad Jammu and Kashmir and two from Islamabad. Moreover, 623 properties were fully damaged and 1,216 partially damaged in rain-related incidents across the country.

Tale of two private jets. This is a tale of two private jets, bought for two chief ministers, on two different continents, in two different worlds. While a debate rages in Pakistan about the purchase and use of a private jet by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, the Premier (chief minister) of Ontario, the largest province of Canada with a GDP of roughly C$900.8 billion (US $643.54bn) in 2017 terms, also had to face a similar outcry when the provincial government announced on April 17 this year, the purchase of a Canada made, ten years old, 2016 model, pre-owned Bombardier Challenger 650 jet for Premier Doug Ford’s “extensive travel(s)”. The jet, bought for C$28.9 million, was to facilitate the Premier’s travel within Ontario and the United States, the announcement said. Announcing the purchase, a spokesperson for the Ontario government then said that the plane would be used solely to conduct “government business”, and not for any personal trip. Premier Ford argued then that the province needed the plane because Ontario is vast, and he needed something more secure to travel to the United States to push back against President Donald Trump’s trade war . Compared to what happened in Pakistan, when the premier of Canada’s Ontario faced backlash over the purchase of a plane, he reversed his decision While defending the purchase, Mr Ford’s office also cited that the plane was necessary for “more certain, flexible, secure and confidential travel,” citing the premier’s trips across the province as well as to meetings with fellow premiers and the prime minister. The purchase resulted in an uproar. Critics quickly derided it as the “gravy plane” — a play on Ford’s boasts in the past that he was elected to “stop the gravy train” of government spending. All guns targeted Premier Doug Ford for the purchase. Ontario Opposition Leader Marit Stiles, of the New Democratic Party (NDP), called the jet a “gravy plane” in a social media post, adding that Ford should be “flying economy like the rest of us.” Premier Doug Ford faced an outcry when the provincial government announced the purchase of a Canada-made, ten-year-old, pre-owned jet for C$28.9 million “I think it’s outrageous that the premier would be considering spending 30 million [Canadian] dollars on a luxury private plane at a time like this — when Ontarians are struggling with the price of rent, the price of food,” Stiles said at an unrelated news conference then. The NDP, in its statement, also cited a 2019 Toronto Star story , in which Ford had said that he was “the only premier in history” who would prefer to drive around the province than spend taxpayer dollars flying. Interim Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser strongly condemned the Ford government’s purchase of the pre-owned Bombardier Challenger 650 private jet, calling it completely “out of touch”. Groups outside of the opposition benches were also quick to denounce the provincial government’s purchase. The Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF) demanded in a statement that Ford reverse plans to spend taxpayer dollars on a private jet. “Instead of taking commercial flights like many premiers in this country do, Ford would rather cosplay the life of the rich and famous on taxpayers’ dime,” said Noah Jarvis, CTF Ontario director. “Ordinary taxpayers are struggling to make ends meet, and (Ontario premier) Ford is making them pay for a personal jet so that he doesn’t have to wait in line at the airport like everyone else.” And with public pressure piling on the purchases, both in Pakistan and in Canada, the outcomes of the two were starkly opposite to each other. Here in Toronto, the outcry forced Premier Ford to change his decision. He had to take a U-turn. Within a few days of the announcement of the jet purchase, Mr Ford gave in, conceding that he had heard the public’s concerns. “Despite the best of intentions, I have heard and agree that now is not the right time for the expense of a government plane. The province is working with Bombardier and other partners to sell the plane as quickly as possible,” he said. Speaking at an unrelated announcement in Ottawa, he then added, “I’m the premier that listens to the people, and if they don’t like something, I’m not too shy to change my mind”. Within days, the plane was sold back to Bombardier at the purchase price of C$28.9 million. But Premier Ford is not out of the woods. The purchase, and the expenses involved in the process, cost the provincial exchequer an additional amount of around C$200,000. He will have to answer that too. Premier Doug Ford is known as a go-getter. He has won three consecutive elections in the province for the provincial Conservatives. Yet, pundits now believe his party may have to pay a political price for the decision to buy a private jet for the premier of Canada’s largest province, which boasts the highest GDP among the provinces of the country. Real democracy is at work — at least here in Canada. The writer is a Canadian-based analyst. X: @rhusainsyed Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, September 28th, 2026

Aleema provided basic facilities, essential items in jail, Punjab govt tells LHC. LAHORE: The Punjab government on Monday told the Lahore High Court (LHC) that Aleema Khan, a sister of PTI founder Imran Khan, had been provided basic facilities and essential items in jail. Aleema was detained on Sep 20 after the Lahore deputy commissioner ordered her detention or arrest under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance. The detention has come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party has postponed to Oct 4. The protest has been called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. Assistant Advocate General Farrukh Khan Lodhi submitted a report on behalf of the Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent during the hearing of a petition filed by Shahrez Khan, Aleema’s son. According to the report, Aleema had been provided with a bedsheet, blanket, shoes, six suits and a towel. She was also given face wash, a toothbrush, a skincare kit and a shawl, it added. In light of the government’s report, Justice Abher Gul Khan disposed of the petition. The judge also directed the home secretary to decide, in accordance with the law, on the petitioner’s request seeking permission to meet Aleema. At the last hearing on Sept 26, Barrister Taimur Malik had told the court that his client, Aleema, was facing difficulties in receiving her medicines and other essentials in jail. Aleema’s sisters, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, have also been detained for 30 days ahead of the PTI’s protest and march to Islamabad. On Sept 24, the LHC turned down a request to immediately suspend the preventive detention notifications issued against Noreen and Uzma.

5 men held over bomb scare at England base used by US to attack Iran are UK nationals: police. Five men held over a bomb scare at a British air base used by the US are all UK nationals aged in their mid-20s, British counter-terror police said Monday. The five — a 25-year-old, three men aged 24 and a 23-year-old — all based in London, have been detained since Sunday on suspicion of offences including “preparation of a terrorist act” under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police. The five were questioned by the police on Monday. Officers detained the group in the early hours of Sunday after they received a tip-off that three large white vans had been seen heading to the military airfield of RAF Fairford in the west of England. US President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and US authorities. However, a local farmer said she had tipped off police after seeing a group of “hooded and masked men” running into the fields. British counterterrorism detectives have publicly shared little about the suspects but a source familiar with the investigation earlier said an Iranian-linked motive was considered the most likely, while a Russian sabotage operation or a terrorism plot were also being looked at as possibilities. B-1 Lancer bomber at the RAF Fairford airbase, after police declared a major incident at the base after several men were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain on September 28, 2026. —Reuters Defence minister Wes Streeting told BBC News on Monday that he would not speculate about motives of a live investigation. But he added on the general Iranian threat to the country: “We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies.” The Iranian embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved in the bomb scare. In an X post, the embassy criticised “the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran” to the incident. In May, Britain sanctioned 12 individuals and entities linked to Iran, accusing them of involvement in hostile activity including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilise the UK and other countries. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in attacks or plots in the UK and elsewhere. Base cordoned off The British government had given authorisation to the US to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The government has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being regularly updated on the incident and he cancelled attending at least two events at his Labour Party’s annual conference on Sunday. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards had warned Britain in July not to allow US bombers to fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target. In Fairford, police have imposed a 400-metre cordon around the base and evacuated residents from 85 homes. A bomb disposal robot could be seen on Sunday operating around the three white vans, while security was stepped up around the base. Armed police stood guard at the main entrance while large machinery was used to block other access points. Security was also stepped up at other US bases in Britain.
