Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel. SUDAN Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says a siege of El Obeid would deepen the humanitarian crisis facing civilians, many of whom have already fled to the city from fighting elsewhere. Meanwhile, the increased use of drones against El Obeid could allow for sustained attacks through the now-beginning rainy season, when ground fighting has typically slowed. 26 June 2026 BOLIVIA President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of exception starting Saturday after more than 50 days of protests triggered by a land reform law and planned austerity measures. Authorities say at least 37 people have been injured in clashes between demonstrators and police. The decree bans the protesters’ roadblocks that have paralysed commercial traffic, causing shortages of basic goods in the administrative capital La Paz, and (temporarily) allows the armed forces to assist police in reopening key routes. It does not, however, suspend fundamental rights, as is often the case with states of exception in Latin America. Before making the declaration, Paz had signed an agreement to “pacify” the country with the biggest trade union, the Bolivian Workers’ Central, which withdrew from the streets. Most of the roadblocks have vanished since the measure took effect. But Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says tensions remain high. The unrest could erupt anew if the government fails to deliver on socio-economic commitments it made to the union or if other groups involved in the protests, including campesinos and Indigenous people, decide to resume the pressure. COLOMBIA Right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella won Sunday’s presidential runoff by the thinnest margin in Colombian history, defeating Iván Cepeda, who had campaigned on continuing leftist President Gustavo Petro’s social reform agenda. De la Espriella styles himself as an outsider. Boasting of his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, who endorsed him before the vote, he has vowed to take an iron-fist approach to organised crime, for instance pledging to bomb narco-traffickers and build mega-prisons. Many Colombians are ready for such measures, says Crisis Group expert Renata Segura, having become frustrated with Petro’s attempts to negotiate “total peace” with criminal and other armed groups. But, as the close vote shows, nearly half the electorate is equally concerned about de la Espriella’s promise to circumvent checks and balances in pursuit of quick fixes. To protect public safety, Colombia needs to balance crimefighting with efforts to plug the gaps in state services that criminal organisations exploit, including for recruitment. The new government should not disregard negotiations, which, if done the right way, have proven an effective tool for reducing violence in Colombia. U.S. - IRAN U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Wednesday that technical delegations from the U.S. and Iran will reconvene at the end of June to resume talks aimed at ending the conflict between the two countries. By the terms of the memorandum of understanding reached between the Trump administration and Tehran in Islamabad earlier this month, these working groups are tasked with negotiating the details leading to a “final deal”, including nuclear commitments by Iran and sanctions relief provisions by the U.S. Maintaining momentum in dialogue is critical, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as the two sides have put forward clashing interpretations of the parameters they agreed to in Pakistan. The negotiations have many moving parts – related to the Strait of Hormuz and Lebanon, among other issues. In this ambitious scope lies promise, but also peril, as a setback on any one front could derail the whole endeavour. 19 June 2026 HAITI Visiting Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Haiti is suffering “the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere”. He toured the headquarters of the new Gang Suppression Force assembled to battle the criminal bands bedevilling the country. The UN released figures showing that gang violence has killed 2,300 people in the year to date and displaced a record 1.5 million more. Gangs have also kidnapped around 100 Haitians, including the defence ministry’s cabinet director last week. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says much hope rests on the new force, but whether it can deliver remains to be seen as it builds toward its mandated strength of 5,500. Gangs, meanwhile, appear to be adapting, attacking senior officials and expanding abductions into formerly safe areas, possibly to deter anti-gang operations where kidnapping victims are held. MYANMAR - CHINA Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Myanmar’s coup-leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit to Beijing this week. The two sides reaffirmed their “community with a shared future” and signed eighteen agreements covering areas including transport and development. The visit highlighted Beijing’s priorities in Myanmar: border stability, protection of Chinese investment, progress on select China-Myanmar Economic Corridor projects and continued cooperation in combating online scams and other transnational crime. Crisis Group expert Richard Horsey says the state visit’s symbolism may matter more than any individual deal, as it provides Min Aung Hlaing with a measure of the international legitimacy he craves. For China, meanwhile, it is an opportunity to lock in a dependency that provides growing strategic opportunities, while it pushes for greater calm in conflict-affected areas along the Myanmar border. UKRAINE - RUSSIA Overnight into Thursday, Ukraine launched its largest drone assault on Moscow since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, hitting an oil refinery and injuring at least seventeen people. Russia said it intercepted 194 drones around Moscow and nearly 1,000 drones and several cruise missiles nationwide over 24 hours. Ukraine said the attack was a response to Russian strikes earlier this week that damaged the UNESCO-listed Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monastery. Moscow warned it would respond forcefully. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says the attacks highlight Ukraine’s efforts to demonstrate it can hit targets far inside Russia using deep-strike drones. But while such attacks create headlines, they have yet to affect the Kremlin’s warfighting ability and may harden support for the war among the Russian public. 12 June 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Pakistan launched air raids Wednesday across the border with Afghanistan, killing 26 Pakistani Taliban fighters, according to Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. The Afghan authorities, however, said the strikes killed thirteen people, including eleven children. The air raids came one day after Pakistani Taliban fighters ambushed a security outpost in Pakistan’s north west, killing six officers. These incidents ended a month of calm in the conflict between the two countries. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says violent flare-ups like these are likely to persist as long as both countries’ security concerns remain unaddressed. IRAN - U.S. The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says an agreement would be welcome if it steadies the shaky truce and gives Washington and Tehran a clear path to future negotiations. Those talks are likely to be fraught, however, and may not guarantee the end of hostilities if certain issues remain unresolved, such as Israel’s continued attacks on and occupation of over 20 per cent of Lebanon. WESTERN SAHARA A Moroccan airstrike on Sunday killed three Polisario Front members who were carrying out an attack on Moroccan fortifications in Western Sahara. Among the dead was Lehbib Mohamed Abdelaziz, son of Polisario’s former secretary general, who had been rumoured to be a candidate to become the Front’s leader. His death marks a major loss for the Polisario. The Moroccan strike came as UN envoy Staffan De Mistura was visiting the Tindouf refugee camps for consultations with the Polisario. Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani says this latest episode shows that negotiations to resolve the Western Sahara conflict are under increasing strain. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. NIGERIA The military announced Tuesday that joint strikes carried out with the U.S. had killed 175 jihadist fighters in the preceding week, in addition to destroying stockpiles of arms. At a hearing in Washington on Tuesday, General Dagvin Anderson, head of U.S. Africa Command, told U.S. legislators that “the epicentre of global terrorism is in Africa”. They are a setback for ISWAP, at least for the time being. U.S. - CUBA The U.S. indicted former Cuban leader Raúl Castro Wednesday for murder and conspiring to kill U.S. nationals. The charges relate to a 1996 incident in which Cuban fighter jets shot at planes flown by anti-Castro Cuban Americans trying to help Cubans escape the island. These legal developments arrive amid renewed speculation that the Trump administration intends to decapitate the Cuban regime much as it did the Venezuelan government with its raid to snatch former President Nicolás Maduro in early January. Senior U.S. officials, most recently Central Intelligence Agency head John Ratcliffe, have held a series of semi-secret meetings with high-ranking figures in Havana this spring. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says any attempt to forcibly break the tight grip the Cuban Communist Party and military have upon the state could result in violent chaos and further suffering for the Cuban people. 15 May 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO A spate of lethal violence in the north-eastern Ituri province over the past two weeks has underscored the complexity of the country’s crisis. In late April, a group of Codeco militiamen killed at least 69 people, mainly civilians, in a series of separate attacks. Allied with the Congolese government, Codeco claims to defend the interests of the Lendu people, most of whom are farmers, from encroachment by ethnic Hema herders. According to local sources, it raided several Hema villages in retaliation for assaults on Congolese army positions by a Hema armed group. The following week, gunmen from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a Ugandan insurgency now affiliated with the Islamic State, killed at least fifteen people in Biakato, an Ituri market town. The province has been under martial law since 2021, the same year that Uganda (with Kinshasa’s permission) sent in troops to pursue ADF militants based in Congolese territory. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. U.S. - CHINA U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded their long-awaited summit Friday. Nor did it bring a major reversal, which some in Taiwan had feared, such as Trump agreeing to scale back U.S. arms sales or change Washington’s longstanding declaratory policies toward the island. First, it underscored Trump’s desire to gain a greater foothold in China for U.S. businesses as well as his conviction that a strong working rapport with Xi can produce a cooperative relationship between Washington and Beijing. ETHIOPIA A showdown may be looming in Tigray, Ethiopia’s northernmost region, after its ruling party reinstated a state council Tuesday that was dissolved immediately before the bloody 2020-2022 Tigray war. U.S. - CHINA Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to host U.S. President Donald Trump in Beijing next week for a long-awaited summit, which had been slated for the end of March. In exchange, Xi may try to extract security concessions from Trump, perhaps by asking him to lessen U.S. defence backing for Taiwan or to declare that the U.S. “opposes“ (rather than “does not support“, which is the longstanding U.S. position) Taiwanese independence. 1 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Fresh violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan erupted this week. Afghan authorities said Pakistani mortars and missiles hit a university and residential neighbourhoods in eastern Kunar province on Monday, killing at least seven people and wounding at least 85. Pakistan denied targeting civilians, saying its strikes aimed at militants, based on intelligence. COLOMBIA Nearly two dozen people are dead and scores injured after a series of apparently coordinated attacks in the country’s south west that authorities blamed on Estado Mayor Central (EMC), a dissident faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. Militants used drones, explosives and roadblocks to hit targets including police stations and military bases. On 25 April, improvised explosive devices went off on a major highway in Cauca, striking a bus and other civilian vehicles, killing at least twenty. ROHINGYA Nearly 900 Rohingya refugees died or were reported missing while trying to make perilous sea crossings in 2025, the UN said last week. It is the highest number ever, representing one in seven of the Rohingya who braved such journeys. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says this grim record points to the increasing desperation among the Rohingya in camps in southern Bangladesh, who are facing cuts to food aid. Unable to go home to Myanmar’s Rakhine State, which is wracked by war, or to work legally in Bangladesh, ever more refugees are trying to escape by boat to Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia. The new Bangladeshi government should permit Rohingya to secure jobs in sectors with labour shortages. The more ways the Rohingya have to earn a living in refuge, the fewer of them will risk their lives at sea. Iran tightened its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz Wednesday, firing on two cargo vessels attempting passage. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. Closing the New War Front in Yemen cthuratong Fri, 09/18/2026 - 13:46 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Internally displaced (IDP) Yemenis who fled their homes due to renewed clashes between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels drive to the safety of al-Kadah in the Taiz Governorate, southwestern Yemen on September 6, 2026. Ahmad Al-Basha / AFP Statement / Middle East & North Africa 18 September 2026 9 minutes Closing the New War Front in Yemen The Houthis’ rapid advance on the western Yemeni coast has opened a new front in the Middle East war that began with February’s U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran. A truce in Yemen is an urgent priority, so that hostilities do not spiral, drawing in more countries. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Yemen Saudi Arabia Iran In mid-September, Houthi rebels charged down Yemen’s western coast, seizing strategic territory from government-aligned forces and turning the country into an active front in the Middle East confrontation pitting the U.S. and Israel against Iran. Their rapid advance has also brought Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, squarely into the region-wide struggle, in which the Houthis side with Tehran . On 11 September, government-linked forces lost the coastal city of Mokha and much of the defensive system stretching from southern Hodeida through western Taiz toward Bab al-Mandab, upending the local military balance and putting the Houthis in a stronger position from which to attack the government’s principal ally, Saudi Arabia, and shipping in the Red Sea. The gains come as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is already bottled up by overlapping Iranian and U.S. restrictions, putting further pressure on world oil markets. The immediate priority should be to reach a truce. Oman, in particular, should use its channels to all sides to achieve a freeze in their positions: the Houthis would halt their escalation both inside Yemen, particularly around Taiz, and against Saudi Arabia; in return, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government would cease all hostilities with the rebels. Iran, which may see benefit in another front heating up, is running considerable risk in further alienating its neighbours. Instead, it ought to use its leverage to push the Houthis in a conciliatory direction – a step it would be far more likely to take amid de-escalation with the U.S. along the lines of the memorandum of understanding, now defunct, reached in June. The next challenge will be to renew talks about a political settlement, backed by confidence-building steps concerning Sanaa airport and the Yemeni economy as well as by Iranian support for reciprocal Houthi restraint. The Houthis Gain a Strategic Foothold The Houthis’ offensive on the western coast marks yet another flare-up of Yemen’s conflict, as the rebels attempt to break a long-running stalemate with the internationally recognised government and its Saudi backers. The surge in fighting began with attacks on 20 July on Saudi territory and Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea, before the Houthis launched a ground assault on government-aligned forces and seized the coastline. The Houthis had previously spent weeks probing the government’s defences. In August, they repeatedly struck the town of Mokha, as well as its port and nearby positions, with ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden boats, while attempting to infiltrate the front line in western Taiz. These preparatory attacks allowed them to identify key defensive positions, gauge reinforcement times and test how government-aligned formations would respond to simultaneous pressure. The decisive battle commenced when Houthi forces moved against the government’s supply lines near Mokha. Advances through the western mountains in Taiz, followed by capture of an encampment used by government-linked forces, threatened the roads connecting Taiz, Hodeida, Mokha and Bab al-Mandab. Once the encampment fell, Mokha lost much of its defensive depth. Withdrawal may have spared government units from encirclement, but it also handed the Houthis a major victory and a foothold farther down the coast. The map shows areas of control and the main front lines in western and eastern Yemen as of September 2026. Source: Crisis Group research / CRISIS GROUP The speed of the coastal front’s collapse reflected a deeper weakness in the anti-Houthi camp. An amalgam of government-aligned forces – the National Resistance, Giants Brigades, National Shield and Taiz axis units – were defending the coast but each with separate chains of command and sources of supply. They were not functioning as a single army with integrated reserves and air defence. These formations historically also had separate relationships with outside patrons. Saudi Arabia supports some of them, but the United Arab Emirates had stood up a number of others, and its withdrawal from Yemen in January, following a falling-out with the Yemeni government and Riyadh, left a political and logistical breach that complicated communications within the coalition. The Houthis exploited the gaps. Once its line began to break, the government had no unified command capable of coordinating retreats, reinforcements or counter-attacks. For the Houthis, the advance’s value lies in the momentum it generates for their domestic agenda, especially in tandem with Iran’s actions in the Strait of Hormuz. They are cash-strapped, but if economic gain had been their principal objective, eastern Yemen would have offered more obvious rewards, given that it comprises the country’s main oil fields. Bab al-Mandab offers something better: influence over a maritime chokepoint at a moment when another, the Strait of Hormuz, is under severe pressure. This influence is powerful leverage for both the Houthis in talks with the Saudi-led coalition arrayed against them and for Iran in its showdown with the U.S. In previous negotiations, the Houthis had sought several measures, such as oil revenue sharing and payment of salaries to civil servants in areas under Houthi control. In 2023, shortly before Hamas’s 7 October attacks derailed the deal, they had arrived at an understanding with the Saudi-led coalition that gave them some of what they wanted, for instance opening Sanaa airport to flights to and from five international destinations. Now, emboldened by their march down the coast, the rebels are demanding the items above, but also much more: an end to Saudi support for the Yemeni government, Saudi withdrawal from Yemen and war reparations. They see cross-border attacks and control of heights overlooking Bab al-Mandab – which allows them to impose what they describe as an embargo on Saudi-linked shipping – as the means of achieving these ends. As for Iran, by compounding the disruption of commerce in the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis’ approach serves the goal of driving up oil prices, thus augmenting international and domestic political pressure on the Trump administration as the U.S. midterm elections in November draw near. High Stakes for the Saudis For Saudi Arabia, the Houthi advance sharpens an increasingly dangerous two-strait problem, in which its ships face peril in both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Riyadh had tried to prepare for this contingency by strengthening Yemeni government forces, building multilateral deterrence arrangements and keeping channels open with the Houthis and Iran. All three elements of this strategy are now under strain. The coastal front’s breakdown exposed the limits of military consolidation, while international backing remains, for now, focused on sharing intelligence and defending the kingdom itself rather than battling the Houthis. Emerging agreements with Pakistan and Türkiye may bolster Saudi surveillance and air capabilities, but they are unlikely to alter the balance inside Yemen. As for the U.S., President Donald Trump has made clear his reluctance to get involved, saying the Houthis reached out before their offensive to assure Washington they were not looking for another fight like that during the 2023-2025 Gaza war, when they last menaced Red Sea shipping in a systematic way. European and Arab powers will likely support Riyadh, though they also have their limits. Finally, Saudi diplomacy with Tehran and the Houthis has clearly not changed these actors’ calculations. For the kingdom, economic stakes are high and rising. The Houthis resumed fire at Saudi-linked vessels in the Red Sea just as they also attacked Saudi energy facilities and Iranian-backed Iraqi Shiite armed groups launched missiles that led to closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline. On 11 September, after the above-ground pumping stations were hit, Saudi Arabia closed the largely underground pipeline. The conduit had been carrying 3-4.5 million barrels per day toward the Red Sea, helping offset the constriction of the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Saudi crude transits through Bab al-Mandab fell from more than 3.5 million barrels per day in early July to near zero in August. Riyadh has been relying more heavily on Egypt, shipping oil by tanker to Ain Sokhna on the Red Sea, then through the Arab Petroleum pipeline 320km north west to the Mediterranean. There, it is reloaded onto tankers headed for Europe, as well as for Asia around the Cape of Good Hope. That lengthy route was already adding time and cost; in addition, too few tankers were available. Even with reports of larger Saudi shipments through Hormuz under U.S. protection, the flow of oil from Saudi Arabia will remain lesser than usual, vulnerable to attack and thus more expensive. The combination of Houthi control of Bab al-Mandab and attacks on energy infrastructure will inevitably have consequences for Saudi Arabia’s economy, regional trade and global energy markets. Riyadh may conclude that it needs a measure of military success to prevent Houthi gains from becoming entrenched and push the group back toward negotiations. It is likely to combine airstrikes on Houthi positions on the western coast with greater support for Yemeni government forces seeking to recover lost ground, while it looks for alternative ways of shipping out its oil. But Saudi Arabia has little appetite for a return to the large-scale operation that proved so costly after it first intervened to reinstate the Yemeni government in 2015. In the absence of active U.S. involvement, its preferred course will be to enlist willing and able regional and European countries in its efforts to defend Red Sea shipping and its territory. It may also seek their logistical support for its airstrikes in Yemen, while leaving the ground war largely to Yemeni forces and trying to revive its diplomacy with Tehran and the Houthis. That approach could contain the immediate threat, but should it fail, a widening campaign could draw Yemen deeper into the Middle East war, expanding it to both shores of the Red Sea and hardening Saudi Arabia’s position toward Iran. A Way Out The danger is that both sides draw the wrong lesson from the latest fighting. The Houthis may conclude that territorial gains and maritime pressure can extract major political concessions, leading them to dig in demanding not just salary payments and reparations but political recognition as a legitimate authority in Yemen. But it is virtually impossible for Saudi Arabia to agree to such steps, which it would see as tantamount to surrender, with all of the attendant political and strategic costs. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government may, in turn, try to reverse their fortunes by enlisting more countries on behalf of their campaign and opening several fronts at once, hoping that the Houthis will relent, notwithstanding the rebels’ record of resiliency under duress. Either course could tip Yemen back toward full-scale war and worsen what is already a catastrophic humanitarian crisis in the country. The first objective should thus be to freeze the military contest in place. That would entail the Houthis halting their offensive in Yemen and stopping attacks on Saudi territory and shipping. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government would refrain from opening new fronts and pair measures designed to defend their positions with steps that offer the Houthis incentives for restraint. These would include allowing regular commercial flights from Sanaa to the five destinations agreed upon in 2023 and progress on economic arrangements such as payment of civil servants’ salaries. Oman is best placed to broker such a deal, while opening space for the parties to return to negotiations on broader political issues. But Iran, too, should realise that the slide toward broader war could jeopardise its remaining contacts with Saudi Arabia and further nudge other regional countries to align against it. Rather than encourage the Houthis along their current path, it should use its leverage to push for a halt to attacks on Saudi Arabia and an end to further territorial conquest in Yemen. Of course, given how closely the Yemen conflict is connected to the U.S.-Iran confrontation, any such de-escalation would be greatly facilitated by easing tensions between Tehran and Washington – and any sustainable de-escalation likely would require as much. Efforts to that end have failed so far, but events in Yemen should serve as a reminder of the urgency. European and regional states should double down on collective efforts to revive a version of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding reached in June, focused on removing the double blockades on the Strait of Hormuz; issuing waivers for Iranian energy exports; and freezing both new U.S. sanctions and Iran’s nuclear program. For all, the aim should be to work in concert to prevent the confluence of the two fronts from provoking an even wider war that could embroil other regional and international actors in the Red Sea.
